source_trace: Claim C1 (encoder-decoder outperform baselines): Table 1 reports 82.72% (best model) vs. 79.91% (bi-LSTM tagger baseline), 77.89% (Norma), 75.72% (averaged perceptron). Section 4.1 claims 'almost all our encoder-decoder architectures perform significantly better than the four state-of-the-art baselines.' No statistical significance testing reported.

Claim C2 (MTL improves without attention): Table 1 shows MTL BEAM+FILTER 82.76% vs. Base BEAM+FILTER 80.46% (2.30 pp gain). Section 4.1 states 'adding attention does not help. In fact, attention hurts the performance of our multi-task architecture quite significantly.' Confound: CELEX (365,530 wordforms) vastly larger than main task (7,350 tokens avg.).

Claim C3 (MTL and attention learn similar strategies): Section 5.1 reports parameter correlation r=0.346 (SD=0.315). Section 5.2 reports error overlap 27.7 shared corrections of 47.7 total, output agreement κ=0.834. Section 5.3 reports saliency correlation ρ=0.615 for longer sequences (≥7 chars), ρ=0.303 (±0.177) for all sequences. Analysis limited to 19,000 word pairs where all models agree.

Claim C4 (attention degrades MTL): Table 1 shows MTL BEAM+FILTER+ATTENTION 82.02% < MTL BEAM+FILTER 82.76% (0.74 pp drop). Section 4.1 claims 'attention hurts the performance of our multi-task architecture quite significantly.' Appendix A (Table 4) shows pattern across 43 texts; some texts show MTL+attention improvement (e.g., D3: 83.20% vs. 82.90%), contradicting 'consistent pattern' claim.

Claim C5 (cumulative gains): Table 1 shows Base GREEDY 78.91% → BEAM 79.27% → BEAM+FILTER 80.46% → BEAM+FILTER+ATTENTION 82.72%. Section 4.1 claims 'beam search, filtering, and attention lead to cumulative gains.' Bidirectional encoding only explicitly used with attention (Section 3.4); unclear if used in base variants.

Claim C6 (first encoder-decoder application): Introduction states 'We are, to the best of our knowledge, the first to propose and evaluate encoder-decoder architectures for historical text normalization.' Section 6 acknowledges Azawi et al. (2013) used LSTMs with alignment layer; distinction from encoder-decoder not clearly articulated.

Claim C7 (2% improvement): Abstract claims '2% increase in performance'; Section 4.1 claims 'almost 3% in absolute terms'; Table 1 shows 2.81 pp improvement (82.72% vs. 79.91%). Discrepancy suggests imprecision in reporting.

Assumption A1 (character-level input sufficient): Section 3.1 states 'By basing our model on individual characters as input, we keep the vocabulary size small.' Section 2 notes 'we also lowercase all characters, since it helps keep the size of the vocabulary low.' Risk: lowercasing may lose information for proper nouns or systematic capitalization patterns.

Assumption A2 (single hyperparameter set generalizes): Section 3.6 states 'We used a single manuscript (B) for manually evaluating and setting the hyperparameters.' Section 4 applies same hyperparameters to 43 test texts. Risk: optimal hyperparameters may differ by dialect, time period, or token count.

Assumption A3 (CELEX appropriate for historical texts): Section 3.5 states 'Our auxiliary task is to predict a sequence of phonemes as the correct pronunciation of an input sequence of graphemes.' Section 2 notes CELEX contains 'phonetic transcriptions of German wordforms.' Risk: CELEX contains modern German; historical phonology may differ substantially.

Assumption A4 (word-level accuracy appropriate metric): Section 4.1 states 'We use word-level accuracy as our evaluation metric. While we also measure character-level metrics, minor differences on character level can cause large differences in downstream applications, so we believe that perfectly matching the output sequences is more useful.' Risk: downstream applications may tolerate minor character-level errors.

Assumption A5 (first-derivative saliency valid): Section 5.3 states 'We follow Li et al. (2016) in calculating first-derivative saliency.' Risk: first-derivative saliency has known limitations and can be adversarially manipulated; alternative methods not compared.

Assumption A6 (lexical filtering unbiased): Section 3.3 states 'For the lexicon, we use all word forms from CELEX (cf. Sec. 2) plus the target word forms from the training set.' Footnote 3 notes 'we cannot reach 2.25% of the targets in our test set, most of which are Latin word forms.' Risk: filtering may exclude valid historical normalizations.

Assumption A7 (correlation indicates functional similarity): Section 5 states 'A possible interpretation of this counterintuitive pattern might be that attention and MTL, to some degree, learn similar functions of the input data.' Risk: correlation does not establish causation or functional equivalence.
Assumption A8 (beam size 5 optimal): Section 3.3 states 'setting the beam size to 5' without justification. Risk: optimal beam size may differ across texts or model variants.

Assumption A9 (1,000 tokens per test set representative): Section 4 states 'using 1,000 tokens each for a test set.' Risk: test set may be too small for reliable performance estimation; results may not generalize to other test sets.

Assumption A10 (14-character word length limit unbiased): Section 3.2 states 'we also set a maximum word length of 14, and filter all training samples where either the input or output word is longer than 14 characters. This only affects 172 samples... and is only done during training. In other words, we evaluate our models across all the test examples.' Risk: train/test mismatch may inflate reported performance.
transparency_notes: Paper is generally transparent about methods, hyperparameters, and evaluation protocols. Detailed hyperparameter documentation (Section 3.6: embedding size 128, dropout 0.3, batch size 50, 50 epochs, learning rate 0.003) and implementation details (Keras v1.0.8) support reproducibility.

Paper acknowledges key limitations: lexical filter removes 2.25% of test targets (Section 3.3, footnote 3); development set reserved but not used (Section 4); maximum word length of 14 characters enforced during training but not testing (Section 3.2).

Paper does not discuss statistical significance testing, which is a critical omission for a paper making empirical claims about performance improvements. No p-values, confidence intervals, or significance tests reported.

Paper does not discuss confounding of MTL improvement with auxiliary task data quantity (CELEX 365k vs. main task 7.3k tokens), which is a significant limitation affecting interpretation of mechanistic claims.

Paper does not discuss limitations of saliency-based interpretability or compare to alternative interpretability methods (integrated gradients, attention weights, layer-wise relevance propagation), limiting confidence in mechanistic analysis.
Paper does not develop theoretical framework for MTL-attention relationship; connection to Caruana (1998) conjecture is mentioned but not formalized.
Paper provides full results for all 43 texts in Appendix A, enabling readers to assess consistency and variability of improvements across diverse texts. This transparency is commendable.
Paper frames mechanistic claims as discoveries ('we put this hypothesis to the test') rather than hypotheses supported by correlational evidence, potentially overstating confidence in findings.
Novelty claim scope is not precisely defined; distinction from prior neural work (Azawi et al. 2013) is unclear, making it difficult to assess novelty claim.
Paper does not discuss generalization to other historical corpora, languages, or tasks, limiting scope of claimed contributions.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper makes solid empirical contributions (systematic evaluation across 44 diverse texts, 2–3% performance improvement, multi-faceted interpretability analysis) but has significant methodological limitations that reduce confidence in specific claims. The central mechanistic hypothesis (MTL learns attention-like mechanisms) is creative but underdetermined by correlational evidence. Recommendation: Accept with major revisions addressing the following critical issues: (1) Conduct statistical significance testing (paired t-tests or bootstrap confidence intervals) for all performance comparisons. Report p-values and 95% confidence intervals. This is essential for establishing whether improvements are statistically reliable. (2) Design controlled experiments isolating MTL improvement from auxiliary task data quantity. Train MTL with CELEX subsampled to match main task size; compare to single-task model with equivalent additional data; compare to other regularization techniques. Clarify which factor (MTL mechanism, data quantity, regularization) drives improvement. (3) Reframe mechanistic claims from causal ('MTL learns attention-like mechanisms') to correlational ('MTL and attention exhibit correlated behavior'). Explicitly discuss alternative explanations (both mechanisms reduce overfitting independently, both exploit sequential structure) and limitations of correlational evidence. (4) Report per-dataset parameter correlations (not just mean and SD) to characterize variability. Investigate sources of variability (text length, dialect, time period). (5) Clarify bidirectional encoding usage across all model variants; add ablation study isolating bidirectional encoding contribution separately from attention. (6) Analyze performance separately for words ≤14 characters vs. >14 characters to assess train/test mismatch impact. (7) Report performance breakdown by sequence length for saliency analysis; investigate why effect is limited to longer sequences (≥7 chars). (8) Discuss potential phonological mismatch between modern CELEX and historical German; test robustness of MTL improvement to this mismatch. (9) Clarify distinction from Azawi et al. (2013) LSTM+alignment approach; narrow novelty claim if appropriate. (10) Analyze errors resolved uniquely by attention vs. MTL to identify systematic differences in error correction strategies. The empirical contribution is valuable and the multi-faceted analysis is thorough; these revisions will strengthen confidence in the findings and clarify the scope of mechanistic claims.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Strengths: (1) Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 44 diverse texts demonstrates consistency and generalization; (2) Multi-faceted interpretability analysis (parameter correlation, error overlap, output agreement, saliency) is thorough and multi-method; (3) Practical solution to small-data problem in historical NLP; (4) Reproducibility (code release, detailed hyperparameters); (5) Realistic evaluation protocol (single hyperparameter set applied to diverse texts). Critical revisions needed: (1) Conduct paired t-tests or bootstrap confidence intervals (1,000 iterations) across the 43 texts to establish statistical significance of performance improvements (2.81 pp, 2.30 pp, 0.74 pp). Report p-values and 95% confidence intervals for all main results. Use Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. (2) Isolate MTL improvement from auxiliary task data quantity via controlled experiments: (a) Train MTL with CELEX subsampled to match main task size (7,350 tokens); (b) Train single-task model with additional main task data (if available) to isolate regularization effect; (c) Compare MTL to other regularization techniques (dropout, weight decay, early stopping) with equivalent model capacity. Report which factor (MTL mechanism, data quantity, regularization) drives the 2.30 pp improvement. (3) Reframe mechanistic claim from 'MTL learns attention-like mechanisms' to 'MTL and attention exhibit correlated behavior.' Explicitly discuss alternative explanations (both mechanisms reduce overfitting independently, both exploit sequential structure, both are suboptimal approximations to same underlying function). Propose future experiments to test causal mechanisms (e.g., intervention studies, mechanistic analysis of learned representations). (4) Report per-dataset parameter correlations (not just mean and SD) to characterize variability. Investigate sources of variability (text length, dialect, time period). Conduct sensitivity analysis: how do results change if only texts with r>0.5 are included? (5) Clarify bidirectional encoding usage across all model variants. If not used in base model variants, add ablation study: (a) Base BEAM+FILTER with unidirectional encoder; (b) Base BEAM+FILTER with bidirectional encoder (no attention); (c) Base BEAM+FILTER+ATTENTION with bidirectional encoder. Report separate contributions of bidirectional encoding and attention. (6) Analyze performance separately for words ≤14 characters vs. >14 characters to assess train/test mismatch impact. Report proportion of test set affected. Consider retraining models without length restriction or evaluating only on words ≤14 characters. (7) Report saliency correlation separately for different sequence length ranges (e.g., 3–4 chars, 5–6 chars, 7–8 chars, 9+ chars). Investigate why effect is limited to longer sequences. Analyze word length distribution in test set. (8) Discuss potential phonological mismatch between modern CELEX and historical German (14th–16th century). Conduct ablation study: (a) MTL with modern German phonology (CELEX); (b) MTL with historical phonology (if available); (c) MTL with random auxiliary task. Analyze whether MTL improvement is robust to phonological mismatch. (9) Clarify distinction from Azawi et al. (2013) LSTM+alignment approach. Discuss whether alignment layer is functionally equivalent to encoder-decoder architecture. Narrow novelty claim to 'first encoder-decoder RNN application' if appropriate, or broaden to acknowledge Azawi et al. as prior neural work. (10) Analyze the 19.7 errors resolved only by attention and 17.7 errors resolved only by MTL to identify systematic differences in error correction strategies. Are there specific error types, sequence lengths, or dialects where mechanisms differ? Consider reporting overlap as percentage of union (Jaccard similarity) rather than percentage of attention's corrections. (11) Conduct ablation study on beam size (k=1, 3, 5, 10) and report results. Analyze whether optimal beam size varies by text characteristics. (12) Test alternative attention mechanisms (multiplicative attention, multi-head attention, scaled dot-product attention) to assess whether MTL+attention performance drop is specific to soft attention or generalizes to other variants. (13) Compare first-derivative saliency to alternative interpretability methods (integrated gradients, attention weights if available, gradient×input). Report whether conclusions hold across methods. (14) Analyze performance breakdown by text characteristics (dialect, time period, token count) to assess generalization. Report whether MTL improvement is consistent across strata or driven by specific subsets. (15) Clarify why development set was reserved but not used. Consider using for hyperparameter tuning, early stopping, or cross-validation. These revisions will strengthen the empirical foundation, clarify the scope of mechanistic claims, and improve confidence in the findings.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
This paper proposes encoder-decoder RNN architectures with multi-task learning for historical text normalization on small datasets (Early New High German, 44 texts, avg. 7,350 tokens). The work achieves 2–3% absolute improvement over prior state-of-the-art (Bollmann & Søgaard 2016: 79.91% → 82.72%) and investigates whether MTL with grapheme-to-phoneme auxiliary data learns attention-like mechanisms, rendering explicit attention redundant. The empirical contribution is solid—systematic evaluation across diverse texts with consistent improvements. The mechanistic analysis is multi-faceted (parameter correlation, error overlap, output agreement, saliency correlation) but relies on correlational evidence. Critical limitations include absence of statistical significance testing, confounding of MTL improvement with auxiliary task data size, moderate correlations with high variability, and correlational rather than causal evidence for mechanistic claims.

Strengths:
- Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 44 diverse Early New High German texts spanning different dialects, time periods (14th–16th centuries), and token counts (4.2k–13.2k), with per-text results enabling assessment of consistency and generalization
- Multi-faceted interpretability analysis combining four complementary approaches (parameter correlation, error overlap, output agreement, saliency correlation) with visualizations, demonstrating thorough investigation of MTL-attention relationship
- Practical solution to small-data problem in historical NLP: demonstrates competitive performance on datasets averaging 7,350 tokens, with character-level input reducing vocabulary and model complexity
- Realistic evaluation protocol: single hyperparameter set tuned on one development text applied to all 43 test texts without re-tuning, reflecting real-world constraints in historical text processing
- Avoidance of explicit character-level alignment: encoder-decoder architecture eliminates need for prior alignment, simplifying preprocessing compared to sequence-labeling baselines
- Reproducibility and transparency: detailed hyperparameter documentation, implementation details, commitment to public code release, and full per-text results support reproducibility
- Insightful visualization of learned representations: t-SNE projections demonstrate that MTL model learns better generalizations compared to base model

Limitations:
- Absence of statistical significance testing: No p-values, confidence intervals, or significance tests reported for any performance comparisons. Improvements (2.81 pp, 2.30 pp, 0.74 pp) may not exceed noise margins. Standard deviations suggest variability; without significance testing, cannot determine if differences are statistically reliable or due to random variation. This is a critical methodological gap affecting confidence in all empirical claims.
- Uncontrolled confounding of MTL improvement with auxiliary task data quantity: CELEX grapheme-to-phoneme data (365,530 wordforms) is ~50× larger than main task training data (7,350 tokens average). Unclear whether MTL improvement is due to (1) MTL mechanism, (2) regularization effect from auxiliary task, or (3) simply having more training data. No ablation study isolates MTL contribution from data quantity effect. This confound directly undermines the mechanistic claim that MTL learns attention-like mechanisms.
- Moderate correlations with high variability across datasets: Parameter weight correlation (r=0.346, SD=0.315) is moderate with estimated range 0.03–0.66 across texts, suggesting weak and inconsistent relationship. Saliency correlation (ρ=0.615) only holds for longer sequences (≥7 chars); effect size for shorter sequences (ρ=0.303±0.177) is substantially weaker. Shared error corrections (27.7) represent only ~58% of attention's total corrections (47.7), with substantial independent contributions remaining. These moderate and variable correlations weaken the claim that MTL and attention learn 'functionally similar' strategies.

Open Questions:
- Are the reported performance improvements statistically significant? Conduct paired t-tests or bootstrap confidence intervals across the 43 texts to establish whether improvements exceed noise margins. Report p-values and 95% confidence intervals for all main results.
- What is the relative contribution of MTL mechanism vs. auxiliary task data quantity to the observed improvement? Design controlled experiments: (1) Train MTL with CELEX subsampled to match main task size; (2) Train single-task model with equivalent additional data; (3) Compare MTL to other regularization techniques. Which factor drives the 2.30 pp improvement?
- Is the MTL-attention relationship causal or merely correlational? The paper presents correlational evidence but does not establish causal mechanism. What alternative explanations can be ruled out? Can intervention experiments distinguish between mechanisms?
- Why does saliency correlation only hold for longer sequences (≥7 chars)? What proportion of test examples have ≥7 characters? How does sequence length dependency affect practical relevance for typical historical words?
- How do results generalize beyond Early New High German? Evaluate on other historical corpora and languages to assess whether findings are language-specific or task-specific.
- What is the impact of uncontrolled confounds on reported improvements? Separately analyze: (1) performance on words ≤14 characters vs. >14 characters (train/test mismatch); (2) performance on words in lexicon vs. out-of-vocabulary (lexical filter removes 2.25% of targets); (3) performance with and without lexical filtering.
- How sensitive are results to hyperparameter choices? Conduct sensitivity analysis: vary embedding size, dropout, batch size, learning rate. Do optimal hyperparameters vary by text characteristics?
- Do alternative attention mechanisms (multiplicative, multi-head, scaled dot-product) show similar degradation when combined with MTL? Test whether MTL+attention performance drop is specific to soft attention or generalizes to other variants.

Transparency:
The paper is generally transparent about methods, hyperparameters, and evaluation protocols. Detailed hyperparameter documentation and implementation details support reproducibility. The paper acknowledges key limitations (lexical filter removes 2.25% of targets, development set not used, train/test mismatch for words >14 chars). However, the paper does not discuss statistical significance testing, confounding of MTL improvement with auxiliary task data quantity, limitations of saliency-based interpretability, or theoretical framework for MTL-attention relationship. The paper frames mechanistic claims as discoveries rather than hypotheses supported by correlational evidence, potentially overstating confidence in findings. Novelty claim scope is not precisely defined; distinction from prior neural work (Azawi et al. 2013) is unclear.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: do not avoid the nonlinear and recurrent computation. In this work, we introduce a new type of lin- ear connections for multi-layer recurrent networks. These connections, which are called fast-forward connections, play an essential role in building a deep topology with depth of 16. In addition, we in- troduce an interleaved bi-directional architecture to stack LSTM layers in the encoder. This topology can be used for both the encoder-decoder network and the attention network. On the WMT’14 English- to-French task, this is the deepest NMT topology that has ever been investigated. With our deep at- tention model, the BLEU score can be improved to 37.7 outperforming the shallow model which has six layers (Luong et al., 2015) by 6.2 BLEU points. This is also the ﬁrst time on this task that a single NMT model achieves state-of-the-art performance and outperforms the best conventional SMT sys- tem (Durrani et al., 2014) with an improvement of 0.7. Even without using the attention mechanism, we can still achieve 36.3 with a single model. After model ensembling and unknown word processing, the BLEU score can be further improved to 40.4. When evaluated on the subset of the test corpus without unknown words, our model achieves 41.4. At the decoding step, the target se- quence is generated from the representationc. Recently, there have been two types of NMT mod- els which are different in the interface part. In the encoder-decoder model (Sutskever et al., 2014), a single vector extracted from e is used as the rep- resentation. In the attention model (Bahdanau et al., 2015), c is dynamically obtained according to the relationship between the target sequence and the source sequence. The recurrent neural network (RNN), or its spe- ciﬁc form the LSTM, is generally used as the basic unit of the encoding and decoding part. However, the topology of most of the existing models is shal- low. In the attention network, the encoding part and the decoding part have only one LSTM layer respec- tively. In the encoder-decoder network, researchers have used at most six LSTM layers (Luong et al., 2015). Because machine translation is a difﬁcult problem, we believe more complex encoding and decoding architecture is needed for modeling the re- lationship between the source sequence and the tar- get sequence. In this work, we focus on enhancing the complexity of the encoding/decoding architec- ture by increasing the model depth. 372 Downloaded

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: us to easily propagate the error gradients from the syntactic task loss all the way back to the characters. To combat the vanishing gradient problem of deep networks, as well as to make better use of available training material, the individual component network’s parameters can be bootstrapped by training them separately on a relevant task, before plugging them in to the larger network for further tuning. For example, the part-of-speech predicting network can be trained to accurately predict parts-of-speech on a relatively large annotated corpus, before plugging its hidden layer into the syntactic parsing network for which less training data is available. In case the training data provide direct supervision for both tasks, we can make use of it during training by creating a network with two outputs, one for each task, computing a separate loss for each output, and then summing the losses into a single node from which we backpropagate the error gradients. Model cascading is very common when using convolutional, recursive and recurrent neural networks, where, for example, a recurrent network is used to encode a sentence into a ﬁxed sized vector, which is then used as the input of another network. The supervision signal of the recurrent network comes primarily from the upper network that consumes the recurrent network’s output as it inputs. 7.2 Multi-task Learning

These connections, which are called fast-forward connections, play an essential role in building a deep topology with depth of 16. In addition, we in- troduce an interleaved bi-directional architecture to stack LSTM layers in the encoder. This topology can be used for both the encoder-decoder network and the attention network. On the WMT’14 English- to-French task, this is the deepest NMT topology that has ever been investigated. With our deep at- tention model, the BLEU score can be improved to 37.7 outperforming the shallow model which has six layers (Luong et al., 2015) by 6.2 BLEU points. This is also the ﬁrst time on this task that a single NMT model achieves state-of-the-art performance and outperforms the best conventional SMT sys- tem (Durrani et al., 2014) with an improvement of 0.7. Even without using the attention mechanism, we can still achieve 36.3 with a single model. After model ensembling and unknown word processing, the BLEU score can be further improved to 40.4. When evaluated on the subset of the test corpus without unknown words, our model achieves 41.4. To combat the vanishing gradient problem of deep networks, as well as to make better use of available training material, the individual component network’s parameters can be bootstrapped by training them separately on a relevant task, before plugging them in to the larger network for further tuning. For example, the part-of-speech predicting network can be trained to accurately predict parts-of-speech on a relatively large annotated corpus, before plugging its hidden layer into the syntactic parsing network for which less training data is available. In case the training data provide direct supervision for both tasks, we can make use of it during training by creating a network with two outputs, one for each task, computing a separate loss for each output, and then summing the losses into a single node from which we backpropagate the error gradients. Model cascading is very common when using convolutional, recursive and recurrent neural networks, where, for example, a recurrent network is used to encode a sentence into a ﬁxed sized vector, which is then used as the input of another network. The supervision signal of the recurrent network comes primarily from the upper network that consumes the recurrent network’s output as it inputs. 7.2 Multi-task Learning

As of January 2024, non-anonymous pre-prints are permitted for ARR, but submissions should still be properly anonymized (e.g., not containing explicit references to the authors’ prior work, acknowledgements, links to non-anonymous repositories or services like Dropbox that may track who opened the link).
